questions.prompt: Explain how GitJira stores the order of cards on its board, then walk through what is written, row by row and in which transaction, when a card is dragged to a new spot in another column and when a new issue is created at the bottom of a column. Why this representation over integer positions, what does one move cost, and where can two cards end up holding the same position?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Position is a base-62 string key and rows sort by plain string comparison; a move computes a key strictly between its new neighbours, so it rewrites exactly one row and never renumbers the rest of the column.

[w3] The alternatives fail on writes: consecutive integers make every insert renumber all rows after it (O(n) writes per move), and gapped integers only postpone that until a gap is used up, while a fractional key always has room for one more key between any two.

[w2] keyBetween emits the neighbours' shared prefix, then averages the next digits when they differ by more than one; when they are adjacent it keeps the lower digit and goes one level deeper with no upper bound, and it refuses outright when the lower key is not strictly below the upper one.

[w3] The client computes the new key from the neighbours it is showing and the server only persists it: the move endpoint receives a column id and a position string, checks that the target column belongs to the same project, and writes both fields.

[w2] One transaction holds the move: the issue's column and position update, plus, only when the column actually changed, a status.changed activity event that records the old and new column names, so the board state and its audit trail commit or roll back together.

[w2] Create appends by reading the column's current highest key and asking for a key after it, and that read happens before the transaction; inside the transaction only the issue number is allocated (an atomic counter increment) and the row and its activity event are written.

[w2] Ties come from concurrency: two creates in one column can read the same highest key and compute the same new one, and two people dropping into the same gap compute the same key from the same neighbours; the ADR accepts a visual tie until refresh for the second case.

questions.prompt: Walk through how GitJira's schema evolved across its migrations: the change of Issue.position to a fractional key, full-text search, the sprint columns, watchers and notifications, and the later performance indexes. For each change, say whether it was additive, what already-running code had to tolerate, and what it would cost to apply the same migration to a large table that is taking writes.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The position change was an in-place type change, not an addition: one ALTER turns the column from a double into text with a new default of 'U'. Existing values become their decimal spelling, which are not keys the base-62 utility would generate, and any instance still writing numbers breaks the moment the migration runs.

[w3] The repo's own later rule is expand and contract: add the new shape beside the old one and dual-write, backfill and switch reads, and drop the old shape only in a later release, so every intermediate state works for both old and new code and a rollback is always safe. Its worked example is exactly this position change.

[w2] Full-text search is additive: a generated, stored tsvector (title weighted above description) that Postgres recomputes on every write, plus a GIN index, so no application code keeps it in sync. On a large live table both steps are heavy: a stored generated column is computed for every existing row as it is added, and a plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes while it builds.

[w2] The sprint change only adds: two nullable columns on Issue and a foreign key that sets sprintId to null when a sprint is deleted, so issues fall back to the backlog instead of disappearing, and older code that never reads the new columns keeps working.

[w2] Watchers and notifications are brand-new tables, the safest kind of change because no running code touches them; the notification row's unique dedupe key turns a retried job's second insert into a constraint hit. The migration was hand-written because Prisma's generated diff fights the tsvector column.

[w2] The performance indexes match the query shape: an index on project, then created-at and id descending, lets the board list walk the index already in order and stop at the limit instead of sorting; on a large live table it should be built CONCURRENTLY so writes are not blocked during the build.

[w1] Migrations run once in the release phase before instances swap, never per instance, which would race; that ordering is what makes 'migrate, then roll code forward or back' safe only when each migration is backward-compatible.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict GitJira's ordering design for a board that grows to 5,000 cards in one column with 50 people dragging at once. What does it buy, where exactly does it break, and what would you add before that day?

keyPoints.text: [w3] It buys contention-free moves: moves of different cards touch different rows, so 50 people dragging different cards never wait on each other, and a move stays a one-row write however long the column gets.

[w3] Equal keys are a trap: the utility throws unless the lower neighbour is strictly below the upper one, so once two adjacent cards share a key, a drop between them fails and that slot cannot be targeted until one of the keys is rewritten. Detect ties and repair them with a rebalance.

[w2] Keys lengthen under repeated insertion into the same gap (5 characters at most after 5,000 random operations, longer for adversarial sequences); the remedy is periodic rebalancing that rewrites a column's keys evenly spaced, a scheduled multi-row write rather than part of every drag.

[w2] The server trusts the client's key: the move schema requires only a non-empty string, so a buggy or hostile client can store characters outside the base-62 alphabet, a very long key, or a key that is not between the neighbours. Validate alphabet and length on the server, or have the server compute the key from neighbour ids.

[w2] No index serves 'this column in position order': Issue is indexed on (project, column) and on (project, created-at, id), so finding a column's last key at create time or listing a 5,000-card column in order sorts that column's rows every time. An index on (column, position) serves both.

[w1] The keys assume byte order of the alphabet digits, then upper case, then lower case, while the server orders them with Postgres text comparison; unless the column uses the C collation, a locale-aware collation can rank mixed-case keys differently from the client's JavaScript sort, so the server's 'last key' and the client's view can disagree.
